rows.method: Linux V4L2 + uvcvideo (buffer timestamps, UVC metadata node, quirks=128, /dev/v4l/by-path)
rows.stack: V4L2 mmap ioctls (pure-Python ctypes drafts) on in-kernel uvcvideo; metadata node /dev/videoN+1 (V4L2_META_FMT_UVC)

sync.value: No: free-running cameras; metadata PTS can only measure offsets
sync.note: Nothing in V4L2/uvcvideo starts exposure; SURVEY: none of the surveyed projects controls exposure start on generic UVC webcams. Only cross-camera measurement anywhere is Windows (REPORT finding 15: C930e libusb SCR minus C922 MF PTS varied with sd 0.54-0.79 ms over 5 runs, provisional, at the method floor). Per-camera clock drift was measured on Windows only: C930e STC +42.3 to +49.5 ppm vs QPC between sessions (docs/usb_camera_report.md); ground-truth PTS rates C930e +35 ppm, C922 -3.9 ppm (VERIFY_method section 5). Computed: ~39 ppm relative drift means two free-running cameras slip a full 33 ms frame roughly every 14 min, so inter-camera phase walks continuously. Not measured on Linux.

timestamp.value: Metadata node gives PTS/SCR + host SOF/ns; untested on Linux
timestamp.note: Kernel source reading (v6.12): default buffer timestamp is CLOCK_MONOTONIC when the frame's first payload is processed, flagged SOE but really host arrival. hwtimestamps=1 (root module param) replaces it with PTS mapped via SCR. The metadata node (no root) gives per-payload PTS, SCR, host USB SOF and host ns, which is the same UVC PTS that scored 0.47-0.68 ms on the Windows C922 (= flash method floor, so an upper bound). Caveats carry over: C930e PTS is a synthetic counter (use SCR/STC), rolling shutter ~30-31 ms per frame, C922 PTS sits near end of exposure. Never run on hardware.

mjpeg.value: Yes per API: raw MJPG mmap buffer bytes; hardware run pending
mjpeg.note: Draft copies bytes straight out of the mmap'd V4L2 buffer (decoded_by_pipeline=false) and flags silent pixel-format fallback. SURVEY [doc]: linuxpy raw buffers, GStreamer v4l2src image/jpeg, FFmpeg -input_format mjpeg. Only a mock ioctl smoke test ran (on Windows), which exercised the YUYV-fallback detection path.

unique_id.value: sysfs serial, else by-path/bus_info port chain; maps to key
unique_id.note: Native: /dev/videoN (unstable), QUERYCAP bus_info (usb-<pci>-<port chain>), /dev/v4l/by-path, by-id, sysfs serial/busnum/devpath. camera_identity.py builds <vid>:<pid>:sn=... or port=pci-<ctrl>/<ports> (bus number dropped). Fake-sysfs plumbing test (WSL2, real descriptor bytes) gave C922 sn=B76395EF and C930e port=pci-0000:00:14.0/2.4 keys, all checks ok, but it is not real hardware. Docs (untested): by-id collides for identical serial-less cameras, use by-path.

bandwidth.value: No for MJPEG: quirks=128 affects uncompressed formats only
bandwidth.note: Kernel source (v3.2 to master): UVC_QUIRK_FIX_BANDWIDTH applies only when the format lacks UVC_FMT_FLAG_COMPRESSED, so MJPEG alt choice should be unchanged; YUYV is affected. This conflicts with Dom's experience that it helps MJPEG (REPORT finding 21). Needs root + rebind. uvc_bw_probe.py 'compare' (MJPEG vs YUYV, with/without quirk, reads uvcvideo trace) is drafted, never run.

exposure.value: V4L2 exposure_auto/absolute set + G_CTRL readback drafted; untested
exposure.note: Drafts set EXPOSURE_AUTO=manual, EXPOSURE_ABSOLUTE (100 us units), EXPOSURE_AUTO_PRIORITY=0 and record readback. Never run. C930e manual exposure was unreliable on every API tested on Windows (MF 1 of 5 runs; libusb pre-commit not applied), so readback alone is not proof; needs a step-response check.

format.value: S_FMT/S_PARM with silent-fallback detection; untested on hardware
format.note: Resolution, fps (S_PARM) and pixel format requested; returned values recorded and a substituted format refuses the run.

focus.value: Not tested: no Linux draft sets focus
focus.note: expected: yes via V4L2 focus_automatic_continuous / focus_absolute (uvcvideo maps CT_FOCUS_*); arduino_sync PLAN uses focus_automatic_continuous on Linux. Descriptors show C922/C930e expose focus_auto + focus_absolute; generic 4C4A:4A55 has no focus control.

rows.costs: No admin for capture or metadata node (video group); root only for quirks/hwtimestamps module params. Pure-Python ioctls, no native deps.
rows.verdict: Likely Linux default (native MJPEG + metadata PTS, no admin) but nothing run on hardware; no bandwidth control for MJPEG.

rows.method: libusb / libuvc (patched) and Rust uvc_iso on Linux via udev rule
rows.stack: libuvc + patch 0001 (or Rust uvc_iso / py-libusb1) on libusb 1.0.27, usbfs access via 70-skellycam-uvc.rules, detaches uvcvideo

sync.value: No: free-running; SCR timestamps measure offsets, cannot align
sync.note: Windows analogue (WinUSB, C930e): cross-camera offset vs C922 MF PTS sd 0.54-0.79 ms, provisional, at method floor. Clock drift as in V4L2 row (C930e STC +42..+49 ppm vs QPC, measured on Windows), so phase walks between free-running cameras.

timestamp.value: PTS/SCR + host first-payload ns; Windows 0.4-0.8 ms MAD (floor)
timestamp.note: Patch 0001 exposes PTS/SCR and CLOCK_MONOTONIC transfer-completion times; 23/23 synthetic payload checks pass in Docker Ubuntu 24.04 (no camera). On Windows WinUSB, SCR scored 0.41-0.74 ms MAD and back-dated arrival 0.39-0.78 ms MAD (method floor). The research identifies no Linux equivalent of the Windows xHCI frame-number/QPC IOCTL for the SCR SOF-to-host map; back-dated arrival is available. Not run on Linux.

mjpeg.value: Yes: raw payload JPEG bytes (measured on Windows, same code)
mjpeg.note: libuvc/uvc_iso stream MJPEG with 0 corrupt frames under strict decode on Windows WinUSB (C930e). Builds on Linux; streaming on Linux untested.

unique_id.value: Port chain without open; serial after open; maps to key
unique_id.note: libusb gives bus, port numbers, address and string-descriptor indices without opening; serial needs libusb_open (works once the udev rule grants rw). On Windows the libusb port chain matched the Windows snapshot for 4/4 cameras; address differed. libusb_identity.py derives camera_identity-style keys. Linux bus number is not stable, so the key must use controller + port chain.

bandwidth.value: App picks alt; no root at run time (Linux untested)
bandwidth.note: Measured on Windows WinUSB, C930e only: 720p30 at alt 5 (800 B), 1080p30 at alt 8 (1600 B) on a static scene; under-provisioning drops whole frames. Linux needs no quirks=128 since the app chooses the alt; USBDEVFS_DISCONNECT has no capability check per source. 3+ cameras on one link never tested.

exposure.value: UVC SET_CUR/GET_CUR works; C930e ignored pre-COMMIT exposure
exposure.note: Windows libusb: exposure set only before stream COMMIT was not applied on the C930e (step rise ~32 ms vs ~12 ms expected). Must re-apply after stream start and verify. Linux untested.

format.value: PROBE/COMMIT selects format, size, fps (measured on Windows)
format.note: Same libuvc negotiation as the Windows runs; Linux untested.

focus.value: CT_FOCUS_AUTO set/readback worked via libuvc (Windows, C930e)
focus.note: Only focus-control test in the research: libuvc on WinUSB set focus_auto 1->0->1 with readback; focus_absolute was read (85, range 0-255) but never set. Linux not run.

rows.costs: One-time sudo to install udev rule + replug; uvcvideo detached while streaming so camera vanishes from V4L2 apps (and its /dev/video node); native C or Rust code.
rows.verdict: Best Linux candidate when bandwidth matters (app-chosen alt, PTS/SCR, native MJPEG); needs a first Linux hardware run.

sync.note: Free-running cameras; no measurement on macOS. Drift caveat as other UVC rows.

bandwidth.note: avf_multi_open.py only records OS default behaviour when N cameras share a hub; never run.

format.note: Resolution/fps via activeFormat and min/max frame duration; whether a compressed (MJPEG) subtype can be kept is the open question. Untested.

focus.note: expected: no UVC focus control through AVFoundation (PLAN: 'AVFoundation has no UVC controls'); IOKit control requests might work, untested.

rows.method: Hardware trigger: Arduino-driven FSIN (InnoMaker OV9281, CT_FOCUS_AUTO trigger mode, MoCapSTR-style sync box)
rows.stack: ATmega328P Timer1 pulses to camera FSIN opto input; trigger mode switched via UVC CT_FOCUS_AUTO through OpenCV DSHOW / V4L2 (planned)
rows.platform: Windows DSHOW + Linux V4L2 (plan v1); macOS out of scope

sync.value: Only method that can align exposure starts; unmeasured, plan only
sync.note: One electrical edge drives every camera's FSIN, so oscillator error is common-mode and exposures can start together; this is the only approach in the research that controls when light is integrated rather than just timestamping it. Unknowns: FSIN-edge-to-exposure skew per camera (plan estimate 'up to ~1 ms', possibly gated by bridge firmware; no vendor/third-party figure found); ~18-20 ms re-trigger lockout (MoCapSTR's own sweeps, not reproduced) caps ~50 fps, and a +0.5% resonator at nominal 50 Hz could make cameras reject different pulses (hence 48 Hz default). OV9281 is global shutter (no ~30 ms rolling-shutter row spread). Needs trigger-capable cameras: C922/C930e/generic have no FSIN. Planned M0 spike: 0-25 ms delayed 50 us flash sweep per camera.

timestamp.value: Frame = pulse index; host-fitted rate; edge latency unmeasured
timestamp.note: Plan assigns pulse index from frame intervals with a 10 s local rate fit plus firmware pulse counter; edges are cycle-exact (62.5 ns) on the Arduino clock but the Arduino clock is not the host clock (resonator +-0.5%, fitted on host). Absolute exposure time = edge + unmeasured FSIN latency. Host arrival via OpenCV (CAP_PROP_POS_MSEC on V4L2) remains arrival time.

mjpeg.value: Orthogonal: plan captures via OpenCV, which decodes
mjpeg.note: Trigger is independent of the capture API; a passthrough stack (MF/PyAV/V4L2) could be paired with it but this is untested.

unique_id.value: Orthogonal; sync box keyed by serial or VID:PID+location
unique_id.note: Camera identity comes from the capture stack; CH340 boards lack iSerial.

bandwidth.value: No effect on USB alt; capture stack decides

exposure.value: Manual exposure required; guard exposure+readout <= 0.8 T; untested
exposure.note: On Linux the vendor order is auto_exposure=1 before focus_automatic_continuous=1.

format.value: Rate set by pulses, <= ~50 fps lockout; stream fps fixed at open

focus.note: expected: OV9281 board has a manual lens without AF; not stated in the research. A camera left in trigger mode looks dead; plan reverts in finally.

rows.costs: Trigger-capable cameras (InnoMaker U20CAM-9281M), Arduino + buffer/ULN2803 wiring (~19 mA per FSIN), ~10 engineer-weeks plan incl. 1-week M0 spike; DSHOW trigger write on a streaming handle unverified.
rows.verdict: Only route that can actually tighten exposure alignment (G1); run the M0 spike (skew, lockout, DSHOW write) before committing.

rows.stack: OpenCV 4.12 VideoCapture(index, CAP_DSHOW) -> DirectShow capture filter (ksproxy) on usbvideo.sys

sync.value: No: free-running UVC; no trigger or start alignment
sync.note: Nothing in OpenCV/DirectShow can start or trigger an exposure. No cross-camera timing was ever measured on this path. Measured frame rates differ per camera (C922 30.00, C930e 30.04, generic 25.77 fps in the DSHOW cells), so the inter-camera phase walks freely. Derived: C922 vs C930e drift by about 1.7 ms/s, a full frame about every 20 s.

timestamp.value: None: POS_MSEC = -1; only host time after decode
timestamp.note: From frames.jsonl: pos_msec is -1.0 on every C922 DSHOW frame, so the only time is the host clock read after read()/decode. Host arrival on usbvideo sits on a ~16 ms grid and scored 4.6-5.0 ms vs the flash ground truth on the MF path (REPORT finding 7). DSHOW arrival itself was never scored against ground truth. capture_backends_review says OpenCV uses the preview pin (no timestamps; web/inferred).

mjpeg.value: No: always BGR, 24.6-40% of a core
mjpeg.note: CONVERT_RGB=0 still returns BGR (size-first) or YUY2 at ~10 fps (fourcc-first). No JPEG bytes in any order.

unique_id.value: Index only; map via cv2_enumerate_cameras path; indices changed
unique_id.note: Open is by DirectShow enumeration index. cv2_enumerate_cameras returns the DevicePath per index, and camera_identity.py lists that dshow_device_path for each serial/port key, so it can be mapped at enumeration time. DShow indices changed (C930e 7->2), and the cv2.VideoCapture(index)->physical camera check was skipped (Kiyo risk).

bandwidth.value: No: usbvideo grants max alt; third camera 'open failed'
bandwidth.note: In the all-3 cells the generic camera, sharing a hub with the C930e, failed to open (finding 4). usbvideo picks the same max alt per camera and mode (32/32). There is no alt-setting knob in DirectShow (SURVEY).

exposure.value: Side-channel DS IAMCameraControl persisted; C930e reads back -5
exposure.note: Exposure was set before each cell by a separate process (mf_mjpeg_capture --controls-only --via-dshow, IAMCameraControl/IKsControl on the DS filter). The setting persisted: C922 and generic read back -7 manual after the OpenCV capture. Only readback, not the exposure effect, was checked on this path. OpenCV's own CAP_PROP_EXPOSURE was never tested. C930e manual exposure is unreliable on every API.

format.value: MJPG 720p/1080p30 if size set before FOURCC; else YUY2 10fps
format.note: Requested modes delivered at full camera rate with size-first order. Fourcc-first reproduces YUY2 at 9.99 fps (verifier). The pixel format reaching the app is always BGR.

focus.value: Not tested: focus only read (C922/C930e on auto)
focus.note: The harness reads CameraControl_Focus but never sets it. C922: range 0-250 step 5, auto. C930e: 0-255, auto. Generic camera has no focus control. expected: settable through the same DS IAMCameraControl side channel; OpenCV CAP_PROP_FOCUS/AUTOFOCUS untested.

rows.costs: None today (pip opencv). Decode costs 24.6-28% of a core per camera at 720p and 37-40% at 1080p. MJPG negotiation depends on property order. Open is by unstable index.
rows.verdict: Fine for preview pixels only: no JPEG bytes, no frame timestamp, no sync or bandwidth control.

rows.stack: OpenCV 4.12 VideoCapture(index, CAP_MSMF) -> Media Foundation source reader (decoding) via Frame Server on usbvideo.sys

sync.value: No: free-running UVC; no trigger or start alignment
sync.note: No cross-camera timing measured on this path. Per-camera rates differ (C922 30.02, C930e 29.93, generic padded to 30 but unique 25.3-25.4 fps), so phase walks.

timestamp.value: POS_MSEC = MF sample time on 16 ms grid; no UVC metadata
timestamp.note: From frames.jsonl: raw (NV12) mode pos_msec deltas are 32/46-48 ms, the MF 16 ms grid. Decode mode gives exact 33.333 ms steps (regularized). MF OS sample time scored 4.4-4.5 ms vs the flash ground truth (C922, finding 7). OpenCV exposes no UVC PTS/SCR.

mjpeg.value: No: BGR (46-156% core) or MF-decoded NV12
mjpeg.note: FORMAT=-1 with CONVERT_RGB=0 returns NV12 as a one-row Mat, not JPEG.

unique_id.value: Index (MF order); map via cv2_enumerate_cameras symlink
unique_id.note: The index equals MFEnumDeviceSources order. cv2_enumerate_cameras gives the MF symbolic link per index, which camera_identity.py lists as msmf_symbolic_link per key. MF indices changed (C930e 7->6).

bandwidth.value: No: max alt granted; third camera fails at first grab

exposure.value: Side-channel IAMCameraControl persisted; OpenCV API untested
exposure.note: C922 read back -7 manual after the MSMF capture. The OpenCV forum reports about 39 s per property set on MSMF (web). C930e is unreliable on every API.

format.value: Size/fps set; generic padded with repeats; raw NV12 17 fps
format.note: 48 of ~300 frames repeated on the generic camera. Raw NV12 on the generic ran at 17.1 fps. Opening a Logitech camera takes 39-41 s.

focus.value: Not tested: never set on any API
focus.note: expected: CAP_PROP_FOCUS/AUTOFOCUS map to IAMCameraControl, subject to the same slow MSMF property sets; unmeasured.

rows.costs: 39-41 s open per Logitech camera. 46-54% (720p) to 143-156% (1080p) of a core per camera. Duplicated frames on the generic camera.
rows.verdict: Rejected: slowest and costliest path, no JPEG bytes, no device timestamps.

rows.method: Media Foundation IMFSourceReader, native MJPG, converters off (+ UVC PTS/SCR via capture metadata)
rows.stack: IMFSourceReader (MF_READWRITE_DISABLE_CONVERTERS) via Windows Camera Frame Server on usbvideo.sys; MFSampleExtension_CaptureMetadata after MetadataBufferSizeInKB0; tools mjpeg/msmf/mf_mjpeg_capture.cpp and timing/src/mf_uvc_timing.cpp

sync.value: No: can measure offsets via PTS, cannot align exposures
sync.note: The cameras free-run; MF has no trigger or start control (inferred). Measured: on MF/PTS (C922+C930e, flash run 1), ground-truth median offsets differ by 0.064 ms, CI95 [-0.11, 0.26]. That reflects where the ROIs fall, not sync accuracy: the offset moves 35 ms across image blocks. Online mapping gives -0.30 or +4.1 ms (VERIFY section 6). Finding 15: C930e (libusb SCR) minus C922 (MF PTS) has a std of 0.54-0.79 ms over 5 runs, provisional. Drift: PTS rate vs ground truth is +35 ppm (C930e) and -3.9 ppm (C922). The C930e has two period modes (998,400 vs ~997,230 ticks). Rates are 30.00 / 30.05 / 25.76 fps, so phase walks about a frame per ~20 s (C922 vs C930e, derived). No run was longer than 30 s.

timestamp.value: UVC PTS <=~0.5 ms (method floor) vs OS 4.4 ms; admin
timestamp.note: C922 PTS: 0.47-0.68 ms std vs flash ground truth, 0.40 ms in one -9 run. That is the method floor (~0.5 ms): a frame counter scores the same. Best scores use a whole-run (non-causal) fit; causal versions give 0.59-1.13 ms. C922 PTS marks near the end of exposure/readout (offset -1.14 x exposure change), and rolling shutter spans ~30-31 ms per frame, so the per-row offset to light-on-glass needs calibration. C930e PTS is synthetic; use SCR, but its exposure was uncertain. OS sample time (= llTimestamp = DeviceTimestamp) is on a 16 ms grid, 4.4-4.5 ms. Metadata needs the MetadataBufferSizeInKB0 registry value (admin) plus a replug per camera. The generic camera was never enabled, so its timing is unmeasured.

mjpeg.value: Yes: camera's own bytes, 100% valid, 0.7-2.2% core
mjpeg.note: Output subtype stays MJPG (no decoder MFT). Generic 1080p frames pass only a lenient decode; strict libjpeg-turbo fails. Frame Server CPU was excluded (needs elevation).

unique_id.value: Symlink -> instance ID -> serial/port key (46/46 checks)
unique_id.note: MF_DEVSOURCE_ATTRIBUTE_SOURCE_TYPE_VIDCAP_SYMBOLIC_LINK embeds the function instance ID, which resolves to the composite ID (serial B76395EF on the C922, hub/port otherwise) and LocationPaths. The symlink itself changed after the C930e WinUSB rollback, but the serial/port key did not, so store the key, not the symlink. Opening by symlink activates only the matched camera (Kiyo never activated).

bandwidth.value: No: max alt granted; 2nd hub camera gets 0x800718CF
bandwidth.note: Max-alt reservations are ~24.5 MB/s each (~62% of a USB 2.0 budget), so effectively one MJPEG camera per USB 2.0 link. The refusal shows only at the first ReadSample. No MF bandwidth knob was found in any surveyed library.

exposure.value: MF-source IAMCameraControl: C922 honoured; C930e 1 of 5
exposure.note: mf_uvc_timing sets exposure via IAMCameraControl obtained from the IMFMediaSource before streaming. C922: readback -9/-7/-6 with luma 24/65/95 and a PTS offset that tracks exposure, so it was applied. Generic: -7 is its range minimum. C930e: reads back -7 but integrated ~a full frame in 4 of 5 runs, possibly LogiTune interference; re-applying after stream start was never tested. The MJPEG-matrix MF cells used the DS-filter side channel instead, so they do not demonstrate MF control.

format.value: Exact native MJPG WxH@fps chosen and read back
format.note: GetNativeMediaType enumeration, then SetCurrentMediaType, then GetCurrentMediaType confirms MJPG at the size and rate. Tested 720p30 and 1080p30 on 3 cameras. The generic camera delivers 25.7 fps when 30 is asked (camera behaviour). C922 720p60 was never captured.

focus.value: Not tested: focus read via MF source, never set
focus.note: The session records focus requested 'auto': C922 range 0-250 step 5, value 40, auto; C930e 0-255, auto; generic unsupported. expected: CameraControl_Focus manual set works through the same interface; unverified.

rows.costs: Needs native code (C++ nanobind extension), or GStreamer mfvideosrc / SDL3 / nokhwa. Depends on Frame Server (CPU unmeasured). UVC timestamps need an admin registry value plus a replug per camera; with a LogiTune veto that once caused MF_E_REBOOT_REQUIRED. Blocking ReadSample needs async reading or a watchdog.
rows.verdict: Best usbvideo path: native JPEG plus UVC PTS timestamps, but no exposure alignment and no bandwidth control.

rows.method: Media Foundation IMFSourceReader with MF's own MJPEG decoder (NV12 out)
rows.stack: IMFSourceReader, native MJPG selected on source, NV12 output (MF decoder MFT) via Frame Server on usbvideo.sys

# RocSync: what it is and how it could help the skellycam USB camera research

Sources: the BAL-ROCS-BUT-COOL/RocSync repo (cloned at HEAD `7d1f73c`, 2026-02-23, with full history), the arXiv preprint, and the published Sensors paper. I read the paper through PMC because MDPI returned 403. Nothing was written to the research folder. The clone is at `C:\Users\Dom\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\c--Users-Dom-GitHub-freemocap-skellycam\4134bbeb-e547-436b-a845-3fc78fe46814\scratchpad\rocsync_dl\RocSync`. Anything marked **unconfirmed** is not backed by a primary source I read.

**Bottom line:** RocSync does not align exposures. It records when each frame was exposed on a visible LED clock and lines the videos up afterwards. As a measurement tool it fills the gap the screen-flash method cannot: no display scan-out, no gamma model, and it reads exposure start and end directly. There are two problems with using the stock device on our cameras:
- **Resolution.** It steps every 1 ms; the paper reports 1.34 ms RMSE per frame. That is coarser than the ~0.5 ms floor of our flash method.
- **Rolling shutter.** Its decoder assumes a global shutter, but our webcams take about 30 ms to read out a frame.

The best fit is probably an ESP32 "RocSync-lite" (Section 6) built for USB webcams, reusing RocSync's ideas and, where it suits, its decoding code (MPL-2.0, which skellycam's AGPL can include).

---

## 1. What RocSync is and how it works

**Origin.** Jaro Meyer (ETH Zurich), Frédéric Giraud (Balgrist/UZH), Joschua Wüthrich (ETH), Marc Pollefeys (ETH), Philipp Fürnstahl (Balgrist/UZH) and Lilian Calvet (Balgrist/UZH, corresponding author). Published as "RocSync: Millisecond-Accurate Temporal Synchronization for Heterogeneous Camera Systems", *Sensors* 26(3):1036, 5 Feb 2026, DOI 10.3390/s26031036. The arXiv preprint is 2511.14948 (18 Nov 2025). The original repo, jaromeyer/RocSync, now says it is deprecated in favour of the BAL-ROCS-BUT-COOL fork.

**Hardware (from the repo's KiCad files and JLCPCB parts database `hw/jlcpcb/project.db`):**
- **Board.** 25 x 25 cm PCB with a central ArUco marker. The decoder uses `DICT_4X4_50`, id 21.
- **LED ring.** 100 dual LEDs in a circle. Each pairs a red LED (HL-A-3528, LCSC C516141) with an IR LED (XYC-HIR76C-LX4, C2988728).
- **Binary counter.** 16 dual LEDs.
- **Corner LEDs.** Four, used to refine the homography. The PCB has 120 dual LEDs in total (100 + 16 + 4).
- **LED drivers.** 8 x TI TLC59283, a 16-channel constant-current shift-register driver (C485815). The corner LEDs use BCR420 drivers.
- **Microcontroller.** WCH CH32V003, a 32-bit RISC-V part (C5299908). Firmware is in `fw/src/main.cpp`.
- **Power.** BQ24075 charger, MT3608 boost converter, USB-C for power only, 604050 LiPo cell.
- **Enclosure.** 3D-printed handle and cover, plus matte smoked film over the LEDs.

**How it encodes time (firmware):**
- Timer1 interrupts at 2 kHz and toggles the shift clock, so one lit bit moves one ring position every 1 ms. One rotation takes 100 ms.
- The counter is shifted out and latched once per rotation, so its resolution is 100 ms.
- 16 bits x 100 ms gives about 109 minutes of unique time. The paper states the same.
- In a frame, the lit LEDs form an arc. The first lit LED marks exposure start and the last marks exposure end, in device milliseconds. The paper's Fig. 2 example decodes as counter 12, LEDs 40–57, meaning 1240–1257 ms.

**Analysis software (`sw/rocsync/vision.py`, `video.py`):**
1. Detect the ArUco marker. The frame is rejected if the marker covers less than 0.2% of the image.
2. Warp the board coarsely to 640 x 640 px.
3. Find the corner LEDs and warp again more precisely.
4. Read each of the 100 ring positions as LED intensity minus a background patch, then apply an Otsu threshold. The frame is rejected unless the lit LEDs form exactly one segment, and also if the segment touches positions 0–1 or 98–99 (the counter may have changed during the exposure).
5. Read the counter the same way.
6. For video, fit a RANSAC line of exposure start against frame index (residual threshold of one frame). Every frame then gets a timestamp in device time, with offset and drift.
- Optional extras export ffmpeg `setpts` commands to resample the videos into sync.
- `process_frame(image, ...)` works on a single image, so it could be called on our own decoded MJPEG frames.

**How cameras are synchronised.** Only after the fact. You show the board to each camera, typically at the start and end of a recording. The cameras do not need overlapping views. Each video gets a line mapping frame index to device time, and videos are aligned or resampled from those lines.

## 2. Claimed accuracy and validation

- **Headline claim:** "residual error of 1.34 ms RMSE across multiple recordings" (both arXiv and PMC).
- **Validation 1, against hardware sync.** Two Azure Kinect DK cameras joined by their sync cable, 1080p30 with 8.33 ms exposure, board about 150 cm away. Five 14-minute runs gave RMSE of 0.38, 1.30, 1.94, 1.73 and 1.37 ms (mean 1.34 ms). The Kinect hardware sync is assumed to be perfect; its own error is not measured.
- **Other experiments are indirect.** They score stereo reprojection error rather than time:
  - GoPro 12 + GoPro 10, 4K60 and 30 fps: mean reprojection error of 1.02 px (30 fps) and 0.95 px (60 fps) with interpolation. Without interpolation, RocSync only ties the light-switch method at 60 fps (1.11 vs 1.11 px).
  - GoPro + fusionTrack IR tracker: 1.81 ± 0.17 px.
  - Four-GoPro hand pose: 4.40 vs 8.80 px.
  - A surgical deployment of 73 recordings from more than 25 cameras, checked by eye.
- **Rolling shutter is not modelled.** PMC quotes: "our current decoding pipeline assumes a global-shutter imaging model". The paper blames most of the Kinect residual on rolling shutter, and its Fig. 7 shows uneven sector spacing. The suggested mitigations are holding the board farther away and relying on redundancy across frames.
- **Exposure range.** "Exposure times of up to 100 ms." Frames whose arc crosses the counter boundary are rejected, so long exposures lose many frames. For example, at E ≈ 31 ms roughly a third of frames are rejected (my estimate from the decoder rules). No minimum exposure is stated. The tested exposures were 8.33 ms, 1/240 s and 1/480 s.
- **Frame rate.** "10 to 1000 fps" is a design claim; only cameras up to 60 fps were tested.
- **Resolution.** Each LED step is 1 ms, so a single frame is quantised to 1 ms. Sub-millisecond reading from partial LED brightness appears only as future work in `sw/README.md`.

## 3. What a build needs

- **Cost.** The paper says "approximately US$20 per unit". The volume and whether that includes the 25 x 25 cm PCB are **unconfirmed**.
- **Fabrication.** The KiCad design targets JLCPCB assembly, with Gerbers and a parts database in `hw/jlcpcb/`. The mechanical parts list is in `hw/README.md`.
- **Firmware toolchain.** PlatformIO with the community `platform-ch32v` (WCH Arduino core), flashed through a WCH-LinkE programmer over SWDIO.
- **Discrepancies I found in the repo:**
  - **The oscillator is not a TCXO.** The paper says TCXO, but the BOM's oscillator part C271645 is a TKD SX25Y024000BC1T, a plain 24 MHz ±10 ppm crystal. `hw/README.md` still lists "Use TCXO for better accuracy" as a TODO.
    - In the paper-era firmware (commit `5d82ddc`, which the paper cites), the only clock setting is `-DSYSCLK_FREQ_24MHz_HSE` in `platformio.ini`.
    - At HEAD, the explicit `SetSysClockTo_24MHz_HSE()` call is commented out. It also uses HSE bypass mode, which suits an oscillator, not a crystal. Whether HEAD actually runs from the crystal is **unconfirmed**.
  - **HEAD firmware and decoder do not match the PCB in the repo.** The KiCad PCB has not changed since the initial commit in 2024-09. HEAD's `vision.py` and firmware expect a newer layout with 20 counter LEDs and a 5th corner LED (commit notes say "RGB tested, IR not tested"). That PCB is not in the repo.
  - **HEAD firmware appears not to compile.** It uses `BUTTON_LADDER_PIN`, which is not defined anywhere; the commit message says "analogRead for the buttons still broken".
  - **What to build from.** For the in-repo PCB, use commit `5d82ddc` for both firmware and software.
- **Using Dom's ESP32 instead.** It cannot be dropped in, because the board has its own CH32V003 soldered on. In principle an ESP32 could drive the same TLC59283 chain (clock, data, latch and blank lines), but 3.3 V logic against the board's driver supply is **unconfirmed**. A small ESP32 design of our own is the more practical route (Section 6).

## 4. License

- **Repo: MPL-2.0** (root `LICENSE`, confirmed in both repos). No source file carries the Exhibit B "Incompatible With Secondary Licenses" notice; the Exhibit B text in `LICENSE` is only the standard template. There are no per-file headers, and the hardware files are covered only by that root LICENSE.
- **Effect for skellycam (AGPL-3.0-or-later).** MPL-2.0 §3.3 allows MPL files to be combined into a larger work under a "Secondary License", and §1.12 names the GNU AGPL 3.0 or later as one. So skellycam can include or import RocSync code. The MPL files themselves stay MPL: changes to those files must be shared as source under MPL. A separate research tool that just pip-installs it is simpler still.
- **Paper: CC BY** (PMC states this). The version, presumably 4.0, is **unconfirmed**. Figures and text can be reused with attribution.
- Using the ideas (moving dot, counter, start/end decoding) in our own design raises no licence issue.

## 5. How it could fill the gaps in this research

**(a) G1: real exposure alignment between cameras.**
- **What it can and cannot do.** RocSync measures alignment; it does not improve it. That supports Dom's assumption: only a hardware trigger (FSIN, `arduino_sync/PLAN.md`) can align exposures.
- **What it fixes.** The flash method (`timing/VERIFY_method.md` §1 and §6) cannot measure alignment, for three reasons: display scan-out, a ~35 ms change in ground-truth offset across image blocks, and the two auto-ROIs sitting at different rows. An LED clock has no scan-out. If each camera sees the board on the same sensor rows, or rows are corrected using a measured line time, the difference between per-frame exposure-start series is the real misalignment.
- **What it would show.** With free-running C922 (30.00 fps) and C930e (30.05 fps), the phase between them should slide through a whole frame roughly every 20 s (expected, not measured). With FSIN, the same setup gives the residual skew.
- **Precision.** Stock RocSync gives 1 ms per frame. Fitting many frames gives a better average offset.

**(b) G2: scoring timestamp sources without a monitor.**
- **What it fixes.** Each frame gets its exposure start and end in device time, with no gamma or brightness model, which `VERIFY_method.md` §1 identifies as what limits the flash method.
- **Limits of stock RocSync:**
  - **1 ms quantisation** (about 0.29 ms std per edge) plus rolling-shutter bias. That is coarser than both our 0.5 ms floor and the 46–66 µs SCR jitter (REPORT finding 13).
  - **No host clock link.** The device clock (±10 ppm crystal) must be mapped to QPC independently, or the slope gets fitted to the source being judged and the test becomes circular again. A slope error of 10 ppm is 0.3 ms over 30 s.
  - **The regularity caveat in `VERIFY_method.md` §3 still applies.** If exposures are truly periodic, a frame counter will score as well as PTS. Only sub-millisecond resolution can show per-frame jitter and whether a source follows it.
- **Still useful as is:** it can settle whether C922 PTS sits at exposure start or end (finding 12, provisional). Change the exposure and see which decoded edge PTS follows.

**(c) Rolling-shutter timing, exposure duration, and checking M1 exposure control.** This is the strongest fit.
- **Exposure duration per frame.** The number of lit LEDs gives the actual exposure of each frame, to 1 ms, independently of the API.
  - This directly tests finding 11: does C930e manual exposure set through MF, DShow or libusb (before or after stream commit) really give about 8 LEDs at 2^-7 s, or about 31 at 2^-5 s?
  - It also catches exposure changing mid-stream and shows whether auto-exposure is really off.
  - The flash method had to assume the exposure and could not check it (`VERIFY_method.md` caveat).
- **Rolling-shutter line time.** The decoded start shifts as the board moves up or down the frame. Per-LED image rows inside one frame also hold this information, but only a custom decoder can use it.

**(d) Long-run drift between free-running cameras.**
- Yes. The device clock is common to all cameras, so its ±10 ppm error cancels between them.
- Showing the board at the start and end (the paper's method) gives mean drift. Leaving it in view of all cameras for the whole run gives the drift profile, for example with temperature.
- Range is 109 minutes with 16 counter bits.

## 6. Limitations, and a better fit for this research

**Why the stock device fits our webcams poorly:**
- **Rolling shutter conflicts with decoding.** Our cameras take about 30 ms to read out a 33 ms frame (finding 12). If the board covers 20–25% of the frame height, the ring spans about 6–7 ms of readout. That biases the start/end decode or splits the lit arc, and split arcs are rejected. Shrinking the board makes detection fail instead.
- **Quantisation.** 1 ms steps against a sub-millisecond question.
- **IR is useless here.** The IR half of each LED is irrelevant to webcams with IR-cut filters (expected, not tested). The decoder only uses the red channel, which is quarter resolution on a Bayer sensor.
- **Brightness.** At very short exposures the 8 kHz PWM on the counter LEDs (50% brightness) could matter. LED brightness at short exposures in a dark room is **unconfirmed**.
- **Other gaps.** No link to the host clock. The repo HEAD is inconsistent with its own PCB (Section 3). The device is a 25 cm battery board with no FSIN output.
- **Not a limitation.** It does not need global shutter or IR to work; those only affect accuracy and modality.

**Suggested ESP32 "RocSync-lite" (a proposal; nothing built or measured):**
- **Lay the LEDs in one horizontal line,** so every timing LED falls on the same sensor rows. This removes rolling-shutter skew from decoding.
  - Put a second bar higher or lower in the frame, or move the board, to measure line time.
  - Use red or white LEDs, not IR.
- **Fast dot:** a moving one-hot dot at 100 µs per step. For example, 100 LEDs give a 10 ms rotation, which suits our 2^-7 s (7.8 ms) test exposure.
  - Drive them from shift registers (74HC595, TPIC6B595 or TLC5916) using the ESP32's hardware timer, or SPI/RMT with DMA for low jitter.
  - Add a slow binary counter that changes only once per rotation. 16 bits x 10 ms is about 11 minutes; use 20 or more bits for long drift runs.
  - Optionally read sub-step timing from the brightness of the two end LEDs. Fully lit and fully dark LEDs in the same frame calibrate the tone curve, avoiding our gamma guess.
- **Host link:** send the device's microsecond clock over USB serial and timestamp it in QPC on the host. A lower-envelope fit gives a device-to-QPC mapping that does not depend on any camera, so G2 scoring stays non-circular. The jitter of USB serial on Windows is **unconfirmed**; the envelope fit tolerates it.
- **Shared timer:** drive the FSIN output from the same timer. That measures FSIN-to-exposure skew and lockout directly, replacing the swept-flash M0 test in `arduino_sync/PLAN.md`.
- **Software:** reuse RocSync's homography approach and `process_frame` structure (MPL), but write our own decoder for the linear layout. It should output start and end per frame, per row band.

Full RocSync remains the right reference if other heterogeneous cameras (GoPros, phones) enter skellycam's scope. Its value there is post-hoc alignment at about 1 ms, which beats audio and timecode by the paper's figures.

## Sources

- https://github.com/BAL-ROCS-BUT-COOL/RocSync (HEAD 7d1f73c): `README.md`, `LICENSE`, `hw/README.md`, `hw/jlcpcb/project.db`, `hw/*.kicad_*`, `fw/platformio.ini`, `fw/src/main.cpp` (also at 5d82ddc), `sw/README.md`, `sw/rocsync/vision.py`, `sw/rocsync/video.py`

rows.platform: Windows 11 (Gerald) only, C930e only; Linux/macOS scripts are drafts never run

sync.value: No: free-running camera; only measures offset (std 0.54–0.79 ms)
sync.note: Standard UVC streaming has no frame-start trigger, so libusb can only timestamp exposures, not align them. Measured: in 5 runs with a fixed region of interest, the C930e (libusb SCR) minus C922 (MF PTS) offset had std 0.54–0.79 ms, which is about the ground-truth floor (REPORT finding 15, provisional). Drift: the C930e STC ran +42.3 to +44.7 ppm vs QPC in runs 2–6 (the doc gives +42.3 to +49.5 across sessions), so it must be refitted per session. Computed: at ~42 ppm the phase walks one 33 ms frame in about 13 min against a nominal-rate clock. The C922's rate on this path and the relative drift between two cameras were not measured. Only a hardware trigger (FSIN) could align exposures (arduino_sync plan, nothing built).

timestamp.value: SCR 0.41–0.74 ms MAD (method floor); IOCTL basis weakened
timestamp.note: SCR mapped to QPC scored 0.41–0.74 ms MAD against the flash ground truth. Back-dated first-payload arrival scored 0.39–0.78 ms MAD and a pure frame-counter model scored 0.36–0.73 ms, so the true accuracy is at most ~0.5 ms and is not known more precisely. Raw libusb host arrival scored 1.0–1.7 ms MAD, against 5.8–6.1 ms MAD for MF OS timestamps in the same runs. SCR and back-dated arrival agree to a median of +0.31 to +0.35 ms with robust sigma 46–66 µs. The xHCI IOCTL_USB_GET_FRAME_NUMBER_AND_QPC_FOR_TIME_SYNC mapping is exact only for ~2–3.5 s after START_TRACKING. Over 20 s it shifted by +53/+117 µs (hc0) and −641 µs (hc1), and the returned QPC was non-causal in 41/396 and 208/396 samples, so the phase-2 agreement needs re-checking over longer runs. The C930e PTS is a synthetic counter, so use SCR/STC. Rolling shutter spans ~30 ms per frame, so the time is per row. C930e only, 30 s runs.

mjpeg.value: Yes: raw camera payload bytes; 0 corrupt in 2,135 strict decodes
mjpeg.note: The bytes come straight from the reassembled isochronous payloads (uvc_frame_t.data), with no decoder in the path. Not hash-compared against MF headers. The first frame after a zero-frame start was once truncated, so check EOI and the error bit.

unique_id.value: Bus/port path + serial read without opening (libusb 1.0.30)
unique_id.note: `uvc_capture_test --list` reported port_path (e.g. 1-13.1.4) for every camera and the C922 serial B76395EF via libusb_get_device_string without opening, plus the Windows instance ID and location path. libusb port chains equal the Windows hub_port_chain for all 4 cameras, so they map directly to the serial/port key in naming/camera_identity.py. USB addresses change between enumerations, so do not use them. The upstream libuvc API itself exposes only bus/address/serial (SURVEY); the port path comes from libusb. Only WinUSB-bound devices can be opened.

bandwidth.value: App-forced alt: 720p30 at alt 5 (800 B), 1080p alt 8
bandwidth.note: These figures are for a static scene. With full-contrast noise on screen, 720p needed alt 6–7 and 1080p at alt 8 fell to 19.2 fps. The C930e streamed at alts 4–8 next to the generic camera (on MF) on the same hub; alt 9 was refused. Delivered fps followed 30/ceil(frame size/slot) in 47 of 48 runs. A refused start is followed by a zero-frame start. Only 2 cameras per link were ever measured; the '3–6 per link' figure is a model estimate. The generic camera has a single alt (3069 B), so it gains nothing.

exposure.value: Works only if re-applied after stream start (C930e)
exposure.note: uvc_set_ae_mode(1) + uvc_set_exposure_abs read back 78 (7.8 ms) even when exposure was not applied. With the controls set only before COMMIT, the flash step rise was ~32 ms; with --controls-after-start (re-applied 0.5 s after start) it was ~12 ms, about the same as the C922. This is the only method in this group where an image-based check showed that exposure took effect. The C922 and generic camera were never tested on libusb.

format.value: MJPEG 480p/720p/1080p at 30 fps via PROBE/COMMIT
format.note: Width, height and fps are negotiated with uvc_get_stream_ctrl_format_size. The harness hard-codes UVC_FRAME_FORMAT_MJPEG, and only 30 fps was run. Other fps values and uncompressed formats are untested (expected: libuvc supports them).

focus.value: Autofocus off/on set and read back; absolute focus never set
focus.note: uvc_set_focus_auto returned rc 0 and auto_cur read back 1→0→1 on the C930e. Absolute focus was read (85, range 0–255) but never set (set_abs_rc −999). Streams with focus pinned were run (stream_q*_fixedfocus), but the effect on the image was not checked directly. This is the only focus-control evidence in the whole libusb group.

rows.costs: WinUSB swap of the composite parent device: admin and one UAC prompt, then a replug. The camera disappears from MF/DShow apps and its microphone (usbaudio) vanishes. Rollback (pnputil /remove-device /subtree + /scan-devices) gives the functions new instance IDs (&0&→&1&), changes the MF/DShow paths, ContainerId and indices, and the MetadataBufferSizeInKB0 registry value must be set again. Native C build (MSVC + 3 Windows shims + patch 0001). libusb enumeration sends GET_DESCRIPTOR to every device, including a faulty one. Tested on the C930e only.
rows.verdict: Reference: the only measured bandwidth control and focus control, sub-ms timing; but driver swap, C930e only, timing basis to re-check.

gaps.item: G1 exposure alignment
gaps.why_unknown: Free-running UVC has no frame-start trigger, so no method in this group can align exposures, and none was tested for it. The only cross-camera figure (C930e libusb vs C922 MF, std 0.54–0.79 ms) measures offsets at the flash-method floor. The relative drift between two cameras was never measured; only the C930e STC vs QPC (+37.7 to +45.9 ppm) was. No independent LED/ESP32 ground truth exists.

gaps.item: C922 and generic camera on WinUSB (phase 3), and 3+ cameras on one link
gaps.why_unknown: Every streaming result is from the C930e only. Phase 3 needs a UAC prompt and replugs and was never run. The 3–6 cameras per link figure is a model estimate.

gaps.item: G2 timing beyond ~3 s
gaps.why_unknown: The xHCI frame/QPC IOCTL mapping drifts after ~2–3.5 s (+117/−641 µs over 20 s, non-causal samples). The 30 s phase-2 runs were never re-checked with periodic re-anchoring.

gaps.method: Python libusb1 streamer, Rust uvc_iso (libusb and rawusb), nusb fork
gaps.item: G2 timestamp accuracy vs ground truth
gaps.why_unknown: None of these was run against the flash ground truth. Only internal consistency was measured (STC-vs-SOF residual ~0.29 ms, i.e. SOF quantization).

gaps.why_unknown: The probe implements only PROBE/COMMIT and streaming; no identity listing or camera controls were written or run.

gaps.item: M1 exposure actually applied to the image
gaps.why_unknown: Only the control readback was checked. All of these set exposure before COMMIT, which libuvc showed is not applied on the C930e. Only libuvc with --controls-after-start was image-verified (flash step rise ~12 ms).

gaps.why_unknown: Only libuvc (uvc_probe_quality) ever set CT_FOCUS_AUTO, and it never set absolute focus. The others either lack focus code or (pyuvc) only list and read the focus controls.

gaps.item: M2 fps other than 30 and non-MJPEG formats
gaps.why_unknown: Every libusb run used --fps 30 and MJPEG. The harnesses hard-code MJPEG.

gaps.why_unknown: The C922 was never bound to WinUSB. libusb 1.0.27/1.0.29 read serials only after opening, and only WinUSB devices open. libuvc's libusb 1.0.30 and patched rawusb did read B76395EF without opening.

sync.value: No: free-running UVC; thread barrier aligns stream start only
sync.note: The probe starts all cameras behind a std::sync::Barrier, which aligns open_stream calls, not exposures. No cross-camera exposure alignment was ever measured through nokhwa. REPORT finding 15 (the only cross-camera figure, 0.54-0.79 ms std of the C930e libusb SCR minus C922 MF PTS offset) used other stacks and is provisional. Per-camera clocks drift: C930e STC +42.3 to +49.5 ppm vs QPC between sessions, and vs ground truth +35 ppm (C930e) and -3.9 ppm (C922), so inter-camera phase walks by about 40 us/s, i.e. a full 33 ms frame in about 14 min. That was measured on MF metadata and libusb, not on nokhwa.

timestamp.value: MF sample time on 16 ms grid; no UVC PTS exposed
timestamp.note: The capture_timestamp equals the MF IMFSample time (QPC domain). Intervals are 32/48 ms (p50 32.0, p99 48.0). Host minus sample time is bimodal (~0.3 ms and ~16 ms modes, a ~12-frame beat). The same MF sample time scored 4.40-4.52 ms std vs flash ground truth on the C922 (finding 7). Not scored against the flash directly through nokhwa. Its Buffer has no access to MFSampleExtension_CaptureMetadata (inferred: the probe could record only capture_timestamp even with MetadataBufferSizeInKB0 set on 10-28).

mjpeg.value: Yes: 593/593, 588/588, 515/515 valid native JPEG at 720p30
mjpeg.note: Needs RequestedFormatType::Exact MJPEG. compatible_camera_formats() hides MJPEG on the Logitech cameras because it keeps at most 2 FourCCs.

unique_id.value: CameraInfo.misc() = MF symbolic link; maps to camera_key
unique_id.note: The symlink contains the video-function instance ID and equals naming's msmf_symbolic_link, so it can be looked up to the serial/port key. The symlink itself is not stable: the C930e's changed &0& -> &1& between the 10-25 and 10-28 nokhwa runs, after the WinUSB rollback (finding 23). Capture opens by CameraIndex::Index, which is unstable. Opening by symlink string was not tested. Listing opens every camera.

bandwidth.value: No alt control; refusal surfaces as 0x800718CF read errors
bandwidth.note: In the all-3 run the generic camera got 0 frames with 'Could not capture frame ... desired bandwidth (0x800718CF)' and read_errors = 17,387,202, a hot error loop. The 'no bandwidth knob' finding comes from source/docs (SURVEY).

exposure.value: Reads back; auto->manual needs side-channel IAMCameraControl on IMFMediaSource
exposure.note: nokhwa's set_control reuses the current auto/manual flag, so it cannot switch auto to manual (source-only: nokhwa-bindings-windows 0.4.6). The probe instead set -7 through IAMCameraControl, QI'd from a separately activated MF media source. nokhwa's camera_control() then read back Manual -7. C922 and generic read back -7 after capture. The C930e read back -5 after every capture, matching finding 11 (C930e manual exposure not reliably applied on any API).

format.value: Exact 1280x720@30 MJPEG works; format list hides MJPEG
format.note: Delivered 29.996/30.06 fps for the requested 30. camera_format() reports '1280x720@1 MJPEG' (wrong fps readback). The format list keeps at most 2 FourCCs, drops H264, zeroes non-integer rates and repeats entries 3x.

focus.note: expected: KnownCameraControl::Focus exists, with the same auto->manual flag limitation as exposure, so it would need the same IAMCameraControl side channel.

rows.costs: Rust crate, no Python package (needs a PyO3 binding). Depends on Frame Server. Listing opens every camera. Exposure needs extra Windows COM code.
rows.verdict: Native MJPEG works, but identity, controls and timestamps add nothing over raw MF; not worth the dependency.

result:
# ESP32 timing and sync test rig: design

Scope: this design replaces or adds to the monitor-flash ground truth (`timing/VERIFY_method.md`). It uses a classic ESP32-WROOM-32 DevKit with Arduino-ESP32 core 3.x, which runs on ESP-IDF 5.x, so the IDF drivers (`mcpwm_prelude.h`, `spi_master.h`, `gptimer.h`) can be called from a sketch. Accuracy figures below are **estimates** unless they cite a measured repo result. Nothing here has been built or measured.

Repo files read: `REPORT.md` (findings 7–15, further investigation 1/6/7), `timing/VERIFY_method.md`, `results/windows/Gerald/RERUN_20261027.md` (goal 2 table), `../arduino_sync/PLAN.md` (§1, §4, §8), `../arduino_sync/REPORT.md` (finding 8).

---

## 0. Why the current method stops at ~0.5 ms, and what the rig changes

From `timing/VERIFY_method.md`:
- The ground truth (GT) is a display step at vblank. The time inside an exposure E = 7.8 ms is recovered from partial brightness f through a gamma model. The model error swings by **+180 to −1000 µs across f**, with opposite signs for rising and falling edges. Even a deliberately circular PTS fit leaves 0.49–0.59 ms. So **~0.5 ms is the method floor.**
- The GT offset varies by **35 ms across image blocks**, from rolling shutter plus display scan-out, and the two cannot be separated. Cross-camera "agreement" was therefore a property of where the ROIs sat (§6).
- The C930e exposure was assumed, not confirmed (REPORT finding 11).

The rig fixes these as follows:
1. **Interpolate brightness only inside a short window.** Any brightness interpolation happens inside a 50–100 µs window instead of inside E, so the same model error shrinks by roughly Δ/E (arithmetic in §E).
2. **No scan-out.** An LED or strobe is lit everywhere at the same instant. Rolling shutter becomes a measured, per-camera line time L instead of an unknown mixed with scan-out.
3. **Measure exposure every frame.** E and the exposure start are measured per frame, so M1 (exposure control) is verified directly instead of assumed.
4. **One ESP32 clock.** Every emitted edge is timestamped on the ESP32's timebase, which can be tied to the host clock (§C).

---

## A. Time-code display (LED bar)

### Encoding

A one-hot "chaser" gives the fine time and a Gray-code counter gives the coarse time. RocSync's design is similar, but a straight bar replaces RocSync's ring because of rolling shutter.

**Why one-hot and not binary for the fine time.** A camera row integrates over [s, s+E]. A binary or Gray fine counter that changes many times during E smears into unreadable grey. With a one-hot chaser stepping every Δ:
- every LED that was on during the exposure appears lit;
- the **first lit LED is the exposure start and the last is the exposure end**;
- the partial brightness of the two end LEDs gives a sub-step fraction.

RocSync decodes this way: the first lit LED is the start and the last is the end (see Sources).

| Element | Count | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Fine bar F | 100 LEDs in one straight line | One-hot, advances every Δ = 100 µs (configurable 50 µs–1 ms), wraps every 100·Δ = 10 ms |
| Coarse counter C | 20 LEDs | Gray code `g = n ^ (n >> 1)` of the F revolution count. It increments when F wraps, every 10 ms, so the range is 2^20 × 10 ms ≈ 2.9 h |
| Fiducials | 4 LEDs, always on (DC) | Bar corners, for homography, tilt and orientation. Only 3 of them need to be asymmetric |
| Total switched channels | 120 | 8 × 16-channel drivers = 128 channels; 8 spare, one used as a "mode" bit (bar/strobe/calibration) |

**Decoding coarse time.** Gray code changes one bit per increment, so an exposure that spans one counter increment shows exactly **one** half-lit bit. The value is then k or k+1, and the F bar says where in the exposure the 10 ms boundary fell. That resolves it for any E < 10 ms, which covers the 2^-7 s = 7.8 ms exposure used in every flash run.
- **Longer exposures** (for example the C930e "long state", about a full frame of 33 ms, RERUN goal 2 table): set Δ = 400 µs, giving a 40 ms span. Precision degrades proportionally.
- **Wraps beyond 2.9 h,** or a frame that cannot be decoded, are resolved from the host arrival time mapped through §C. ±5 ms is enough.

### Geometry for rolling shutter

- **Orient the F bar horizontally, along image rows.** All 100 LEDs then fall in one row band and share one exposure window. RocSync's ring spans many rows. Its authors attribute their residual error (mean RMSE 1.34 ms on Azure Kinect) mainly to rolling shutter, and list compensation as future work.
- Put the Gray row directly below the F row, within a few image rows. The single-bit Gray ambiguity rule tolerates the small row offset.
- **Tilt and per-LED row correction.** On the C922, L ≈ 30.8 ms / 720 rows ≈ **43 µs per row**, using the measured 30.1–31.5 ms rolling-shutter span (REPORT finding 12). A bar tilted 1° over 400 px spans about 7 rows, which is a 0.3 ms ramp along the bar. The decoder therefore takes each LED's centroid row from the fiducial homography and moves each LED's sample to a reference row, using the L measured in strobe mode (§B).
- **Physical size.** 100 LEDs at 2.54 mm pitch is a 254 mm bar. For decoding, aim for ≥ 4 px per LED in every camera, so the bar should span ≥ 400 px. At 720p that means about half the frame width.
- **Optional second F bar** at the other end of a tall board, driven by the same channels (two LEDs in series per channel on a 9–12 V LED rail). It gives exposure windows at two rows per frame, and so a per-frame line-time check. This is a v2 feature, not required.

### Rise/fall time, LED choice and drive

- **Drivers.** Use 16-channel constant-current sink shift registers with a latch: STP16CP05, TLC5926 or MBI5026, daisy-chained.
  - All outputs change together on the **LE (latch) edge**. LE comes from a hardware timer, so update instants have no software jitter.
  - The next pattern is shifted in between latches: 128 bits at 10 MHz = 12.8 µs, well inside a 100 µs step.
  - Output switching on these parts is in the 0.1–1 µs range (estimate; check the chosen part's datasheet for t_r/t_f and any staggered output delay). Either way it is **≪ 100 µs**.
- **LEDs.** Use **monochrome AlGaInP red or InGaN green, not white**. White LEDs rely on a phosphor, and some phosphors (for example KSF red) decay over milliseconds. Bare-junction LEDs switch in tens of ns. Diffused 3 mm THT or 0805 SMD both work.
- **Do not use WS2812/SK6812/APA102 addressable LEDs.** They PWM-dim internally at hundreds of Hz to kHz and update through a serial pixel chain, so on a short exposure they show bands and have unknown latency.
- **Never dim by PWM**, either by OE-PWM or in firmware. PWM modulates light in time, which is the very thing being measured. Set brightness with the driver's single R_ext resistor (a trimmer). For partial-brightness interpolation the LEDs must stay unsaturated, so turn R_ext down until the brightest LED sits at about 70% of full scale at the chosen gain.
- **Brightness against short exposure.** An F LED is on for only Δ, so its signal is I × Δ whatever E is, while ambient light grows with E. Work in a dark room with high gain, auto-exposure off, auto-white-balance off, and anti-flicker (power-line frequency) off.
  - **Estimate:** a 20 mA high-brightness LED for 100 µs is clearly visible to a webcam at gain in the dark.
  - **This must be checked first** in phase 0 (§F P0), before building 120 channels.

---

## B. Strobe mode (the main precision instrument)

A single high-power monochrome LED, pulsed for w = 20–200 µs, lights a **matte white card that fills the full image height of every camera**. The F bar can be mounted on the same card.

**Why it works.** Row r exposes over [s0 + r·L, s0 + r·L + E]. A strobe at t_s lights only the rows whose window contains t_s. Each camera therefore shows a **horizontal lit band**:
- bottom edge r_b = (t_s − s0)/L, so **s0 = t_s − r_b·L**, the exposure start of row 0, in ESP32 time;
- top edge r_t = (t_s − E − s0)/L, so **E = (r_b − r_t)·L**.

L comes from a **double strobe** in one frame, with two pulses Δt apart (for example 10 ms): L = Δt / (band separation in rows). It can also come from a slow phase sweep.

What it gives:
1. **G1, real exposure phase across cameras.** One flash is seen by every camera at the same physical instant, with no scan-out and no dependence on rig position. s0_A − s0_B (mod frame period) is the true exposure-phase difference, per frame, over time.
2. **M1, exposure verification.** Band height gives the exposure actually applied, frame by frame, including the frame where a control change takes effect.
3. **Rolling-shutter line time** L, the readout time H·L, linearity (check that L is constant down the frame), and vertical blanking. When E < T − H·L, there are strobe phases that produce no band.

**Equivalent-time sweep.** Set the strobe period to T_cam·(1 + δ), for example δ = 10^-3. The strobe phase then walks about 33 µs per frame and covers a full frame in about 1000 frames (33 s at 30 fps). Free-running drift (tens of ppm) also sweeps it, but slowly.

**Identifying which strobe made a band:**
- Encode identity in the pulse pattern: single pulse versus double pulse with a variable gap.
- Or use the coarse time from the LED bar or host arrival (±5 ms is enough at a 30–40 ms strobe period).

**Light budget.** Every lit row gets the full pulse energy whatever E is.
- **Estimate:** 0.5–1 A into a 1–3 W green star LED (no phosphor) at 0.3–0.5 m from the card, at ≤ 1% duty, gives a strong band at moderate gain.
- Calibrate the camera's tone curve with the strobe itself. Sweep w from 10 to 200 µs at fixed gain; integrated light is proportional to w, so this measures the response curve directly. That removes the a-priori gamma assumption that dominated the flash method's error (`VERIFY_method.md` §1 and §3: "the gamma used matters more than the source").

**ISP artefacts to detect:**
- Temporal noise reduction shows as a weak echo band at the same rows in frame n+1.
- Sharpening causes edge overshoot; use the 50% crossing of a smoothed profile.
- MJPEG 8×8 blocks and chroma subsampling cost some sub-row precision. Repeat key runs in YUY2 at the same resolution, but **L must be measured in each format, resolution and fps actually used**, because a sensor may change readout timing with mode.

---

## C. Tying ESP32 time to host time (QPC / CLOCK_MONOTONIC)

**One timebase.** The ESP32's MCPWM capture timer (APB-clocked; 80 MHz on the classic ESP32) is the timebase. Every edge that matters reaches a capture input through a **loopback wire**: the LE anchor, STROBE, FSIN, and the start bit of each incoming serial ping. These are timestamps of the physical edges, not of the commands. The LE/PWM generators and the capture timer both derive from the same 40 MHz crystal through the PLL, so their ratio is fixed. Verify the timer clocking and capture width in the ESP32 TRM; the IDF page states that the capture resolution equals the APB clock on ESP32.

**Crystal.** ±10 ppm is the commonly cited tolerance for Espressif 40 MHz crystals, but it is **not confirmed for the classic ESP32 or for this DevKit** (forum posts only). It does not matter much: a 10 ppm offset is 0.33 µs per 33 ms frame, and the rate is fitted against the host clock anyway. Over minutes the thermal drift should be < 1 ppm once warm (estimate). Warm the board up for about 5 minutes before runs.

| Option | Hardware | Expected absolute accuracy (estimate) | Expected repeatability (estimate) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. LED/strobe only, relative (as today) | none extra | none: one offset fitted per source per run | at the rig floor (§E) | Scores regularity and inter-camera phase. Cannot give absolute latency (light → host). Sufficient for G1 and M1 |
| 2. Serial ping, min-RTT filter, classic DevKit through CP2102/CH340 | none | ±0.1–0.5 ms unknown bias. The path asymmetry is bounded only by RTT_min/2, likely ~0.5–1 ms | ~20–100 µs after min-filtering thousands of pings | Host stamps QPC at write and read. The ESP32 stamps the **RX start-bit edge** on a capture input (not the UART ISR, which fires on FIFO threshold or timeout) and the TX start bit of its reply. Full-speed bulk through a hub's transaction translator quantizes delivery (probably 125 µs / 1 ms steps). FTDI-style latency timers (16 ms default) must be set to 1 ms. No published µs RTT figures for CP2102/CH340 were found, so measure it. The DevKit resets on port open; re-anchor after each open (as PLAN.md §5.2 already assumes) |
| 3. Native USB CDC ping (ESP32-S3 USB-OTG or USB-Serial-JTAG; C3 USB-Serial-JTAG) | S3/C3 board | similar to option 2, slightly better (no UART hop) | ~10–50 µs | Still bulk scheduling; same asymmetry problem |
| 4. **USB SOF lock (ESP32-S3)** | S3 on the **same xHCI controller** as the cameras | ~1–10 µs to the USB frame clock; to QPC limited by the IOCTL mapping (below) | ~1 µs | The S3 timestamps every 1 ms SOF: poll the USB-Serial-JTAG `FRAM_NUM` register (11-bit SOF frame index, present on S3/C3) on core 1, or use a TinyUSB SOF callback on the OTG port (verify API). The host maps frame number to QPC with `IOCTL_USB_GET_FRAME_NUMBER_AND_QPC_FOR_TIME_SYNC`, already used in phase 2. Caveat, measured: REPORT finding 14 found that mapping exact for only ~2–3.5 s, then drifting up to −641 µs over 20 s, and Microsoft documents its predicted accuracy in 125 µs units. **Re-anchor every ≤ 2 s**, and treat the residual as part of the result |
| 4b. SOF domain without QPC | S3 | ~µs | ~µs | UVC SCR pairs camera STC with SOF number. With ESP time ↔ SOF from option 4, camera STC → SOF → ESP time → LED/strobe truth is a chain that **bypasses QPC and the IOCTL drift**. Not usable on the C922, whose device SOF counter is broken (884/s, `VERIFY_method.md` §5); usable on the C930e |
| 5. GPIO into audio line-in (WASAPI QPC position) | sound card | unknown, not researched | unknown | Mentioned only for completeness |

**Recommendation:**
- Start with **options 1 + 2** on the classic DevKit. Option 1 is enough for G1, M1 and line time; option 2 gives sub-ms absolute latency.
- Add **option 4/4b with an ESP32-S3-DevKitC** (about $10–15) when G2 needs absolute latency at the tens-of-µs level.
- Run options 2 and 4 together once. The S3 SOF path then measures the bias of the serial-ping path, so later runs with only a classic ESP32 can be corrected.
- On Linux, ping options 2 and 3 work as on Windows with CLOCK_MONOTONIC. No user-space frame-number ↔ monotonic API was identified in this research (not checked).

---

## D. FSIN trigger output (InnoMaker OV9281 and others)

- Same MCPWM group, a third timer and generator. The period is set in ticks of the same timebase, and FSIN edges are looped back to a capture input, so **FSIN, strobe and LED code share one clock**.
- **Period.** Choose an integer multiple of the LED step so FSIN stays phase-locked to the code. For example 208 × 100 µs = 20.8 ms (48.08 Hz). That clears the ~18–20 ms InnoMaker lockout noted in PLAN.md §1, with the ESP32 crystal contributing ~0 rate error (the 48 Hz default in PLAN.md keeps the margin).
- **Electrical.** The InnoMaker FSIN is an opto input, about 19 mA at 5 V, triggered on the rising edge (PLAN.md §2). A 3.3 V GPIO cannot drive it. Wire FSIN+ to +5 V and FSIN− to a low-side sink: one AO3400A or 2N7002 per camera, or a ULN2803A channel (PLAN.md §4 electrical table). The GPIO going high turns the opto on; check which optical edge the camera triggers on.
- **Skew measurement** (PLAN.md §8 and arduino_sync REPORT finding 8: "unknown, could be up to ~1 ms"). With the strobe band method, **one frame** gives s0 of the triggered camera relative to the captured FSIN edge, so FSIN→exposure skew and its spread across cameras come out per frame. The sweep is needed only to cover blanking. This replaces PLAN.md's planned "delayed 50 µs flash swept 0–25 ms" with a faster equivalent.

---

## E. Expected ground-truth floor: arithmetic (all estimates)

| Error term | Flash method today | Rig, strobe band | Rig, LED bar |
|---|---|---|---|
| Light source timing | vblank fit, 10 µs residual, plus **unknown** scan-out position and LCD response (folded into the 35 ms block variation) | captured edge, ±12.5 ns; MOSFET + LED rise < 1 µs (constant) | LE hardware edge; driver + LED < 1 µs (constant) |
| Brightness-model error | ~1.2 ms peak-to-peak over f, at E = 7.8 ms (`VERIFY_method.md` §1) | edge ramp is only w/L ≈ 50/43 ≈ 1.2 rows; tone curve calibrated by strobe-width sweep | interpolation inside Δ only: 1.2 ms × Δ/E = 1.2 ms × 100/7812 ≈ **15 µs p-p**, likely less with the calibrated curve |
| Quantization | — | row: 43/√12 ≈ 12 µs per edge before sub-row fit; averaging across hundreds of columns gives an estimated ~3–8 µs | one-hot step: 100/√12 ≈ 29 µs without interpolation; ~5–15 µs with |
| Rolling-shutter / position term | **35 ms** variation across blocks, mixed with scan-out | none for s0 (row 0 by construction); L error × r_b. With L to 0.1% (10 ms double strobe ≈ 233 rows, ±0.3 row per edge), the error at row 360 is ~15 µs, and smaller when referenced near the band | L × residual row error after tilt correction: ±0.5 row ≈ ±20 µs unless corrected |
| MJPEG / ISP blur | gamma confounded | ~5–10 µs (estimate) | ~5–10 µs |
| **Per-frame total (1σ)** | **~0.5 ms floor (measured)** | **≈ 10–20 µs** | **≈ 15–30 µs** |
| Host-time mapping (G2 absolute only) | QPC native (display) | +0 (option 1, relative) / +0.1–0.5 ms bias (option 2) / ~1–10 µs plus re-anchored IOCTL residual (option 4) | same |

So the rig's estimated floor is **~20–50× below the flash method** for relative timing, G1 phase and E. For absolute latency it is set by the §C option. This is fine enough to settle REPORT finding 9: whether C922 PTS is really better than a frame counter. The current data cannot tell them apart (both score 0.5 ms), but the C922 PTS ±0.27 ms alternation (`VERIFY_method.md` §3) would be clearly resolved.

---

## F. Test protocols and host analysis

### Protocols

**P0, bring-up** (one evening; strobe parts only; worth doing before the bar is built):
- Logic-analyzer or loopback check of LE, STROBE and FSIN timing.
- Strobe band visible on all three cameras (C922, C930e, generic) at 720p30 MJPEG, at w = 50 µs, in the dark.
- Echo-band check (temporal noise reduction).
- Measure L for each camera.

**P1, line time and readout map** (per camera × format × resolution × fps):
- Double strobe (Δt = 10 ms, w = 50 µs), 300 frames.
- Outputs: L, H·L, linearity residual, vertical blanking.
- Modes: 480p/720p/1080p, 30/60 fps where available, MJPEG and YUY2.
- Expected (labelled): the C922 matches 30.1–31.5 ms at 720p30 (REPORT finding 12). Other modes are unmeasured.

**P2, M1 exposure verification** (includes the C930e re-apply open item, REPORT further investigation 6, PROGRESS section E):
- For each API path (MF IAMCameraControl / DirectShow / KS property, and libusb SET_CUR), set exposure at these moments:
  - (a) before stream start or COMMIT;
  - (b) 0.5 s and 2 s after the first frame;
  - (c) every 5 s, alternating between 2^-9 and 2^-6.
- Record per-frame E from band height, plus the API readback.
- Outputs:
  - did the requested E apply, and in which frame;
  - control-to-effect latency in frames;
  - whether the readback lies (the C930e read back −7 while integrating about a full frame, RERUN goal 2 table).
- Repeat with LogiTune's updater stopped.
- Also log the C930e PTS period mode (998,400 vs ~997,230 ticks per frame) to test the open hypothesis that the mode follows the exposure state.
- **M3 side-check:** with focus fixed, the LED spot size in the bar is a per-frame sharpness metric. Step manual focus through the values and confirm the spot size changes and then stays put. This detects autofocus that was not actually disabled.

**P3, G2 timestamp scoring:**
- C922 + C930e (+ generic), 60 s × 5 runs, at three exposures (2^-9, 2^-7, 2^-5).
- Log every source: MF OS time, host arrival, UVC PTS/SCR from MF metadata, and on WinUSB the libusb SCR and back-dated first payload.
- Truth per frame: s0 (row 0 exposure start), plus mid-exposure and end-of-readout derived from E and L.
- Score each source three ways:
  1. offset-only std/MAD (comparable with today's tables);
  2. causal online mapping;
  3. **absolute latency** (source − exposure start), using §C option 2 or 4.
- Also: regress PTS − s0 on E to test "C922 PTS near end of exposure" (−1.14·ΔE, provisional in REPORT finding 12), and run 60 s windows to re-check the SCR→QPC basis (REPORT further investigation 1).

**P4, G1 sync phase and drift:**
- All cameras view the card; one strobe per ~frame, with δ-sweep off.
- Δφ_AB(t) = s0_A − s0_B (mod T) over 30 min.
- Fit relative rate (ppm), wander, and any lock.
- Variants:
  - simultaneous versus staggered stream start;
  - same hub versus different root port (tests the hypothesis that a camera derives frame timing from USB SOF, which would give 0 ppm relative drift);
  - each capture API.
- **Expected:** free-running, unaligned exposures drifting at tens of ppm. This is inferred from the GT-derived PTS rates of +35 ppm (C930e) and −3.9 ppm (C922) against QPC (`VERIFY_method.md` §5), which would mean a full-frame slip in roughly 20–30 min. That supports Dom's assumption that no USB-side API aligns exposures. The rig measures phase; it does not align it.
- Report the residual after best software pairing: up to T/2 per frame pair, uniform.

**P5, FSIN** (when OV9281s are available): FSIN→exposure skew per camera, its spread across 4 cameras, and the lockout found by sweeping the FSIN period.

### Host analysis code (Python; new `timing/rig/`)

1. **Event-log parser** for the ESP32 serial stream:
   - `S k t_rise t_fall` (strobe), `F k t` (FSIN), `A n t` (LE anchor), `P seq t_rx t_tx` (ping), `E code n` (missed SPI deadline or other fault), `B boot_id`.
   - Use protocol-2 framing from arduino_sync PLAN.md §3 (`<PROTO:2>`, tagged OK/ERR lines) so the serial driver can later be shared with skellysync.
2. **Clock correlation:**
   - min-RTT and lower-envelope filtering of pings;
   - piecewise-linear ESP→QPC fit over a sliding 10 s window, with uncertainty;
   - optionally the SOF-based mapping, re-anchored every ≤ 2 s.
3. **Frame I/O:** strict libjpeg-turbo decode (REPORT finding 19); the camera's frame index, drops from PTS slots, and the per-source timestamps of each frame.
4. **Tone-curve calibration** from strobe-width sweep frames (integrated light ∝ w), per camera at fixed gain.
5. **Strobe band detector:**
   - card ROI → per-row mean across columns;
   - dark subtraction using rows outside the band, or the previous frame;
   - linearize;
   - 50% edges with sub-row interpolation;
   - flag clipped bands (top or bottom edge outside the frame) and echo bands.
6. **Band → strobe assignment** by coarse time (bar Gray code, or mapped host arrival) and pulse pattern.
7. **Per-frame solve:**
   - s0 = t_s − r_b·L and E = (r_b − r_t)·L;
   - L per camera and mode from double-strobe frames, or by regressing r_b on t_s across a sweep;
   - linearity residual.
8. **LED bar decoder:**
   - fiducials → homography → per-LED disc sampling and centroid row;
   - all-on and all-off reference frames (firmware `<ALLON>`/`<ALLOFF>`) to normalize;
   - first and last lit F LED with fractional ends;
   - Gray decode with the single-ambiguous-bit rule;
   - row-correct each LED with L.
   - Output (t_start, t_end) at the bar's row.
9. **Cross-check:** compare bar-derived and strobe-derived s0 per frame. Their difference is an independent estimate of the rig floor.
10. **Scoring and sync reports:** per-source residual std/MAD, causal versus whole-run fit, absolute latency, Δφ_AB(t) with drift fit, per-frame E against requested E.
11. **Synthetic self-test:** render frames from known s0, E, L, w, gamma and MJPEG quality, and check that the decoders recover them. This mirrors `selftest_flash_analyze.json`. The scorer is cleared to run on real data only after it recovers the synthetic truth within the §E budget, so the circularity issues of `VERIFY_method.md` §1 cannot reappear: the truth uses no camera timestamp at all.

### Firmware outline (classic ESP32, Arduino-ESP32 3.x calling IDF 5 APIs)

- **Wi-Fi and Bluetooth off.** Timing work is pinned to core 1.
- **MCPWM group 0, timer 0, the LE master.** Resolution 10 MHz, period 1000 ticks = 100 µs. A generator makes a 1 µs LE pulse at timer zero.
- **`on_empty` ISR** (IRAM): n++, then notify a top-priority render task on core 1. The task builds the 128-bit pattern (F one-hot plus Gray(n/100)) and sends it with `spi_device_polling_transmit` (VSPI, 10 MHz, 16 bytes) before the next LE.
  - A "done" flag is checked in the next ISR; a miss emits `E`. A missed deadline latches stale data, so it is detectable and flagged, never silent.
- **Timer 1, strobe.** 1 MHz resolution, so periods up to 65.5 ms fit a 16-bit tick count; whether the period register is 16-bit on this part should be verified in the TRM. Width and phase are set by command. Firmware refuses w > 500 µs or duty > 1%.
- **Timer 2, FSIN** at the commanded period.
- **Capture channels:**
  - cap0 ← STROBE loopback;
  - cap1 ← FSIN loopback (used for the LE anchor at start-up, before FSIN is enabled);
  - cap2 ← UART RX start bits.
  - Capture ISR: extend the timer to 64-bit and queue the event for serial output at 921600 baud.
- **Commands:** `<STEP:us>`, `<STROBE:period_us,width_us[,gap_us]>`, `<SWEEP:ppm>`, `<FSIN:period_us,width_us>`, `<BAR:0|1>`, `<ALLON>`, `<ALLOFF>`, `<PING#seq>`, `<STATUS>`.
- **No autostart.** All outputs are off at boot (see pull resistors in G).

**ESP32-S3 changes:**
- MCPWM ×2 groups, RMT and LCD_CAM are present (LCD_CAM could DMA the bar pattern with zero CPU, as a v2).
- Native USB enables §C options 3 and 4.
- Strapping pins are 0, 3, 45 and 46. Avoid 19/20 (USB D−/D+), 26–32 (flash), and 33–37 on octal-PSRAM modules (N8R8/N16R8).

**ESP32-C3 changes:**
- **No MCPWM**, so no capture peripheral. LE would come from LEDC and strobe from a gptimer alarm ISR (about µs of jitter, not loop-back captured).
- Single core.
- Strapping pins are 2, 8 and 9; USB is 18/19.
- Usable for the bar, weaker for strobe and timebase. **Use the S3 instead.**

**LED rail and thermal.** With red V_f ≈ 2.0 V on a **3.3 V LED rail**, headroom is about 1.3 V. At 20 mA that is 26 mW per lit channel, so 16 lit channels dissipate about 0.4 W per driver. A 5 V rail would dissipate about 1 W per driver with all channels lit, which is too hot in SOIC.

### Safety and electrical notes

- **Never drive LEDs from GPIOs directly.** GPIOs drive only the driver logic and MOSFET gates.
- **Strobe current.**
  - Pulse current is limited by a resistor; firmware caps width (500 µs) and duty (1%).
  - Hardware backstops: the 100 kΩ gate pull-down covers boot and reset, and the polyfuse limits a stuck-on gate. A stuck gate at 1 A would put about 1.8 W in the resistor and about 3 W in the LED, so the fuse matters.
  - Check the LED datasheet's pulsed-current rating.
- **Eyes.** Do not stare into the strobe from close range. Avoid IR emitters: they are invisible and webcam IR-cut filters block them anyway.
- **Ground and supply.**
  - Common ground between the ESP32 and the LED and strobe supplies.
  - Keep strobe return current away from the ESP32 ground (star point at the supply).
  - FSIN optos isolate the cameras.
  - Do not feed the rig's LED current through the PC's USB.
  - If the ESP32 shares a hub with cameras, note that its full-speed serial or CDC traffic is negligible bandwidth. For SOF lock it **must** be on the same controller as the cameras under test (Gerald has two controllers, REPORT finding 14).
- **Signal integrity.** For 8 chained drivers over about 30 cm at 10 MHz, keep CLK short, add series termination, and put 0.1 µF at every chip.

## How RocSync relates

**What RocSync is.** 100 red+IR LEDs in a ring stepping 1 ms per LED (100 ms per revolution), plus a 16-bit binary counter. A RISC-V MCU with a TCXO, battery powered. An offline Python decoder takes the first and last lit LEDs as exposure start and end. Per-camera drift is fitted linearly with RANSAC, from showing the clock at the start and end of a session. The authors report mean RMSE **1.34 ms** against hardware-synced Azure Kinects, with rolling shutter uncompensated and named as the main residual. Published in Sensors 2026, DOI 10.3390/s26031036.

**How it helps:**
1. It validates the one-hot "first/last lit LED" encoding used in §A.
2. It is a field-ready, ~1 ms post-hoc sync method for real skellycam sessions, including heterogeneous cameras (GoPro, phones) that never need to view the clock at the same time. Worth evaluating as a user-facing tool.
3. Its TCXO is a good idea for the field version. It is not needed for the bench rig, where the clock is fitted against the host.

**Why it is not the bench instrument here:**
- 1 ms steps are 10× coarser than needed.
- The ring spans image rows, so rolling shutter enters the result.
- There is no host-clock link, so absolute latency cannot be scored.
- There is no strobe or exposure-mapping mode.

The rig in this design is a bench version of the same idea: a horizontal 100 µs bar, a strobe, host correlation and FSIN. Its bar could also run a "1 ms step" mode for field use, but RocSync's decoder assumes a ring geometry, so it would not be reused directly. The RocSync license was not checked; check its LICENSE file before reusing any code or hardware files.

## Suggested build order

1. **Phase 0: strobe only.** One MOSFET, one LED, a white card, about $10. This alone answers G1 (phase and drift), M1 (actual E, C930e re-apply) and line time, at an estimated ~10–20 µs.
2. Serial ping correlation (§C option 2).
3. LED bar (§A), as an independent second method and for coarse time.
4. ESP32-S3 SOF lock (§C option 4/4b), for absolute G2 latency at the µs level and to calibrate the ping path.
5. FSIN outputs when the OV9281s are available.
